methods.title: Methods
methods.intro: Every study follows the same rules. They are strict on purpose: we would rather reject a small real effect than ship a lucky one.

items.name: Data
items.text: Free daily data: about 23 ETFs, the S&P 500 with point-in-time membership from 1996, and public macro, exchange and grid data. Each result records its download date.

items.name: Execution
items.text: Signals use the close. Trades fill at the next open, less 7 bps per trade.

items.name: Testing
items.text: The pass bar and trial count are fixed before each run. Learned models train walk-forward; rules have no fitted parameters. To pass, an idea needs net Sharpe above 0.40, deflated Sharpe above 0.95, a bootstrap 5th-percentile Sharpe above 0, and correlation with the book below 0.3.

items.name: Paper trading
items.text: Survivors trade daily on a simulated broker. Each day must reconcile: cash plus positions equals equity, and profit equals the change in equity.

limitations.title: Limitations
items: A fixed cost per trade, not a model of intraday execution.
Many delisted stocks are missing from the S&P prices, which flatters single-stock results.
The live record starts in June 2026, too short to confirm a Sharpe ratio.

glossary.text: Mean daily return over its standard deviation, annualised. Above 1 is strong for a diversified book.
The fall from a previous peak. Worst drawdown is the largest in the test.
The probability that the true Sharpe beats the best expected from the same number of noise trials, adjusted for sample length, skew and fat tails. The bar is 0.95. (Bailey and López de Prado 2014)
How often the setting that is best on some blocks of history ranks below the median on the rest. (Bailey et al. 2017)
Each model is fitted only on data before the period it trades, then refitted as time moves on.
Daily returns cut into one-month blocks and reshuffled into thousands of histories. The 5th-percentile Sharpe shows a bad-luck outcome.
The same reshuffled histories with the average return removed. A real edge ends above most of it.
Only stocks in the index on each date, including ones later removed.
A second model that decides whether to act on a fixed rule's signal, rather than predicting prices.
How often a classifier ranks a winning trade above a losing one. 0.5 is a coin flip.
The four tests listed under Testing. An idea must pass all four to join the book.
A cheap test, fixed in advance, that can stop an idea before a full backtest.
The gap between a futures price and the spot price it settles to.
What a battery would earn knowing the next day's prices, under the same charge limits. Capture is the share a rule earns.
